seo.h1: Skilled Migration to Australia: Choose Your Visa Pathway

hero.h1: Skilled Migration to Australia: Choose Your Visa Pathway
intro: Australia invites skilled people to live and work here permanently. There are three main points-tested visas, and the right one depends on your occupation, your points and where you are willing to live. Our registered migration agents in Melbourne and Adelaide explain each option in plain English and tell you what to do next.

sections.name: Who this is for
sections.h2: Is skilled migration right for you?

blocks.x: Skilled migration suits you if you have a qualification and work experience in an occupation Australia needs. Most people fall into one of three groups. The requirements are set out in [how skilled migration works](/skilled-migration).

items.x: **Graduates studying or working in Australia.** You may hold a Temporary Graduate visa (subclass 485). You can use Australian study points, regional study points and a state nomination. See [Temporary Graduate visa (485)](/migrate-to-australia/temporary-graduate-visa-subclass-485).
**Skilled professionals overseas.** You have a degree and several years in fields such as health, engineering, IT, teaching or accounting. You will need a skills assessment before you can be invited.
**Tradespeople.** Electricians, chefs, mechanics, carpenters and plumbers need a trade skills assessment from the assessing authority for your occupation.

blocks.x: Not sure which group you are in? [Book a consultation](/book-an-appointment) and we will check.
Select a visa name to open its guide.

blocks.x: Ask yourself these questions in this order.

items.x: **Is your occupation on the Skilled Occupation List?** Use our [Occupation Finder](/occupation-finder). If it is not, 189 is not available.

**How many points do you have?** Use the [PR Points Calculator](/migrate-to-australia/pr-point-calculator). A high score may support 189. A lower score may still work with the extra points from a state nomination.

**Will a state nominate your occupation?** States publish their own lists and requirements. For [Victoria, try the Victorian Points Test](/migrate-to-australia/victorian-points-test). For [South Australia, see South Australia state nomination](/south-australia-state-nomination).
**Are you willing to live in a regional area?** If yes, 491 may give you more options. Check a [suburb with the Postcode Checker](/postcode-checker).
**Do you need a faster, safer route?** A registered agent can compare your realistic pathways. No one can promise an invitation.

faqs.q: What is the easiest skilled visa to get?
faqs.a: No skilled visa is easy, and none is guaranteed. The best route depends on your occupation, points, age and willingness to live outside a capital city. A registered agent can compare them for you.

faqs.q: What is the minimum points score for skilled migration?
faqs.a: You need at least 65 points to submit an Expression of Interest for 189, 190 or 491. (Source: Department of Home Affairs, checked 12 November 2026.) In practice, invitations often go to higher scores.

faqs.q: Do I need work experience to apply?
faqs.a: Not always. Points for skilled employment are optional. Some graduates reach a competitive score through English, Australian study, regional study and other points. You still need a positive skills assessment.

faqs.q: Is the 485 visa a permanent visa?
faqs.a: No. It is a temporary post-study work visa. It can help you gain experience and a skills assessment for a points-tested visa.

faqs.q: What is the difference between 190 and 491?
faqs.a: Both need nomination. The 190 is permanent and gives 5 points. The 491 is provisional, gives 15 points and requires you to live and work in a designated regional area.

faqs.q: Can I include my partner and children?
faqs.a: Usually yes, as secondary applicants. Your partner may also add points if they meet the criteria.

faqs.q: How long does it take?
faqs.a: It depends on the assessment, invitation round and visa processing.

faqs.q: Can you guarantee an invitation or visa?
faqs.a: No. Only the Department of Home Affairs or a state government decides. We tell you honestly what is realistic.

cta.text: Bring your qualifications, work history and English test result. We will help you choose your pathway and next step.

seo.title: How Skilled Migration Works in Australia | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: How Australian skilled migration works: skills assessment, points, SkillSelect and invitations. Plan your PR with a Melbourne migration agent.
seo.h1: How Skilled Migration to Australia Works

hero.h1: How Skilled Migration to Australia Works
intro: Skilled migration is a points-based system. You prove your skills, claim your points, express interest and wait for an invitation. This guide explains each stage so you know what to expect before you spend money. Want to compare the visas themselves? Go to our [skilled visa options](/migrate-to-australia).

sections.name: The system in one minute
sections.h2: The skilled migration system in four steps

items.x: **Skills assessment.** An assessing authority confirms your qualification and experience match your occupation.
**Points.** You claim points for age, English, qualifications, experience and other factors.
**Expression of Interest (EOI).** You lodge an EOI in SkillSelect. This is not a visa application.
**Invitation and visa application.** The Department of Home Affairs, or a state or territory, invites the highest-ranking people. Only then can you lodge a visa application.

blocks.x: The three points-tested visas are the Skilled Independent (189), Skilled Nominated (190) and Skilled Work Regional (491). They are also called General Skilled Migration (GSM).

sections.name: The five requirements
sections.h2: What you must have before you can be invited

items.x: **Age under 45** when you are invited.
**Competent English** at minimum. IELTS 6 in each band, or an equivalent test score, is the usual benchmark.
**A suitable skills assessment** for an occupation on the relevant list.
**At least 65 points.** (Source: Department of Home Affairs, checked 12 November 2026.)
**An invitation to apply.** You cannot lodge a 189, 190 or 491 without one.

blocks.x: You and any family on your application must also meet health and character requirements.

sections.name: Points test overview
sections.h2: The points test at a glance

blocks.x: Points are claimed in your EOI and checked at the time of invitation. Here is the overview. For the full table and a worked example, [read how points are calculated](/skilled-migration/how-points-are-calculated).

head: Factor
Points range (summary)
rows: Up to 20 points, overseas and Australian combined
Australian study, regional study, Professional Year, NAATI, specialist education

blocks.x: Figures as per Department of Home Affairs points table.
**Do I need years of work experience?** No. Skilled employment adds points but is not compulsory for the points test. Many graduates score through English, Australian study and regional study.

Your nominated occupation must be on the Skilled Occupation List that applies to your visa. Each occupation has an assessing authority, for example Engineers Australia, ACS, VETASSESS or Trades Recognition Australia. Assessment can take weeks or months, so start early.
State and territory governments also publish their own lists for 190 and 491 nominations. These can differ from the national list.
Use the [Occupation Finder](/occupation-finder) to find your occupation code and assessing authority.

sections.name: SkillSelect and invitations
sections.h2: What happens after you lodge an Expression of Interest

blocks.x: SkillSelect ranks EOIs by points, then by the date you reached that score. Invitation rounds depend on the number of places for each occupation. A high score does not guarantee an invitation, and a score of exactly 65 is rarely enough in a competitive occupation.

State nomination works separately. Each state invites people from SkillSelect to apply for nomination, using its own criteria. For [Victoria, see the Victorian Points Test](/migrate-to-australia/victorian-points-test). For [South Australia, see state nomination](/south-australia-state-nomination).
Your EOI stays valid for a limited period.

items.x: Claiming points you cannot prove with documents.
Claiming English points from a test that has expired.
Choosing an occupation by interest, not by evidence of your actual duties.
Assuming a 485 visa leads straight to PR.
Missing the age cut-off by a few days.
Ignoring a partner's skills or English, which can change your score.
Compare the visas in [skilled visa options](/migrate-to-australia).
Check your occupation with the [Occupation Finder](/occupation-finder).
Estimate your points with the [PR Points Calculator](/migrate-to-australia/pr-point-calculator).
Read the [step-by-step migration process](/migrate-to-australia/migration) to plan documents and costs.

blocks.x: A registered agent can review your qualifications, points and evidence before you spend money on tests or assessments. We cannot promise an invitation or a visa.

faqs.q: What is General Skilled Migration?
faqs.a: It is the group of points-tested visas for skilled workers: subclasses 189, 190 and 491.

faqs.q: Is an EOI the same as a visa application?
faqs.a: No. An EOI tells the Department you are interested. You can apply for the visa only after an invitation.

faqs.q: How many points do I need?
faqs.a: At least 65 to submit an EOI. Invitations often need more, depending on the occupation and round.

faqs.q: Do I need a job offer?
faqs.a: Not for 189, 190 or 491. These visas are not employer-sponsored. For [employer routes, see employer-sponsored visas](/employer-sponsored).

faqs.q: Can I improve my score?
faqs.a: Often yes. Higher English, a Professional Year, regional study, NAATI credentials and a partner's skills can add points. See [how points are calculated](/skilled-migration/how-points-are-calculated).

faqs.q: How long does the whole process take?
faqs.a: It varies widely. Skills assessment, invitation and visa processing each take time. See the [step-by-step guide](/migrate-to-australia/migration).

faqs.q: Can you guarantee an invitation?
faqs.a: No. We do not guarantee outcomes.

seo.h1: The Migration Process to Australia: Step by Step

hero.h1: The Migration Process to Australia: Step by Step
intro: Moving to Australia as a skilled worker takes several stages, and each one has its own rules. This guide walks you through them in order, from checking your occupation to arriving on your visa. It shows what you do, what the Department does and where people usually lose time.

blocks.x: This is the general skilled route. Employer-sponsored and partner visas follow different steps. See [employer-sponsored visas](/employer-sponsored) and [family visas](/family-visa).

items.x: **Choose your pathway.** Decide between 189, 190 and 491. Your occupation, points and willingness to live regionally drive this choice. Read the [visa comparison](/migrate-to-australia).

**Check your occupation.** Search the [Occupation Finder](/occupation-finder). Note the code and the assessing authority. If your occupation is not on any list, ask us about other options before you spend money.
**Take an English test.** Competent English is the minimum. Higher scores earn points. Book early, because results are valid for a limited time.

**Get a skills assessment.** Apply to the assessing authority for your occupation. You will usually provide identity documents, qualifications, transcripts, employment references and payslips or tax records. Processing times vary by authority.

**Calculate your points and lodge an EOI.** Use the [PR Points Calculator](/migrate-to-australia/pr-point-calculator) and read [how points are calculated](/skilled-migration/how-points-are-calculated). Lodge your Expression of Interest in SkillSelect. You need at least 65 points.

**Get nominated (190 and 491 only).** Apply to a state or territory under its own rules. See the [Victorian Points Test](/migrate-to-australia/victorian-points-test) and [South Australia state nomination](/south-australia-state-nomination).
**Receive an invitation and lodge your visa.** You have a limited time after an invitation to lodge. Pay the visa application charge and upload your documents.

**Complete health and police checks.** You may need health examinations and police certificates for every country where you lived for a set period. See our [AFP police check](/afp-national-police-check) and [Indian police check](/indian-police-check) pages. After the decision, check your visa conditions and the date by which you must first enter Australia.
Passports for every applicant

Degree certificates and academic transcripts
Employment references, contracts, payslips and tax records

Police certificates and health examination results (when requested)

blocks.x: Gather these before you need them. Gaps in employment evidence are a common cause of delay.
Time and cost depend on the pathway, so we do not give a single number.

sections.name: Mistakes that cause delay or refusal
sections.h2: Mistakes that cause delay or refusal

items.x: Starting with the visa and leaving the skills assessment until late.
Claiming points you cannot prove.
Letting an English test expire.
Using an occupation that does not match your real duties.
Not disclosing earlier visa refusals or character issues.
Missing the deadline after an invitation.

blocks.x: If a visa is refused, review rights are time-limited. See [visa refusal](/appeals/visa-refusal).

Once you hold an invitation and a visa, see the guide for your visa: [189](/migrate-to-australia/skilled-independent-visa-subclass-189), [190](/migrate-to-australia/skilled-nominated-visa-subclass-190) or [491](/migrate-to-australia/skilled-work-regional-provisional-visa-subclass-491). Regional visa holders can later apply for the [191](/migrate-to-australia/permanent-residence-skilled-regional-visa-subclass-191).

You can lodge applications yourself. People often ask for help when their occupation is borderline, they have a past refusal, their work history has gaps, or they want to compare 189, 190 and 491. Our registered agents explain the options and the risks. You decide whether to engage us.

faqs.q: How long does the Australian PR process take?
faqs.a: It varies. Add the time for skills assessment, waiting for an invitation, nomination if needed and visa processing.

faqs.q: What is the first step?
faqs.a: Check your occupation and its assessing authority. Then check your points.

faqs.q: Do I need an agent?
faqs.a: No, but a registered agent can help avoid costly mistakes.

faqs.q: Can I apply from inside Australia?
faqs.a: Yes. Many 189, 190 and 491 applicants are in Australia on a student or Temporary Graduate visa. See [485 eligibility](/migrate-to-australia/temporary-graduate-visa-subclass-485).

faqs.q: What if my points are below 65?
faqs.a: You cannot lodge an EOI. You may improve English, gain experience or consider a regional route.

faqs.q: Is a job offer needed?
faqs.a: Not for these visas.

faqs.q: Can my family come with me?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Partners and dependent children can be included.

intro: A permanent visa for skilled workers. You do not need an employer or a state to nominate you. You must be invited, and you can then live and work anywhere in Australia.

blocks.x: The Subclass 189 is a permanent visa. You do not need an employer or a state to nominate you. You must be invited. After the visa is granted, you can live and work anywhere in Australia.
Most people apply in the points-tested stream. Your job must be on the skilled occupation list, and you need a suitable skills assessment.
There is also a Hong Kong stream for people who hold a Hong Kong passport or a British National (Overseas) passport and meet the residence rules. The New Zealand stream is closed to new applications.

faqs.q: What is the Subclass 189 visa?
faqs.a: The Subclass 189 is a points-tested permanent residency visa for skilled workers not sponsored by an employer, state, or family. It allows you to live, work, and study anywhere in Australia permanently.

faqs.q: How many points do I need for a 189 visa?
faqs.a: You need a minimum of 65 points to submit an Expression of Interest (EOI). However, higher scores (80-90+) are often required in competitive occupations like IT, engineering, and healthcare.

faqs.q: How do I apply for a 189 visa?
faqs.a: The application process involves a skill assessment, an English test, submitting an Expression of Interest (EOI) on SkillSelect, waiting for an invitation, and applying within 60 days of the invitation.

faqs.q: How are invitations issued under the 189 visa?
faqs.a: Invitations are issued through SkillSelect, ranked by points. The Department of Home Affairs conducts invitation rounds based on occupation ceilings and current demand. Occupations in high demand may receive more invitations.

faqs.q: Can I include my de facto partner or children in the application?
faqs.a: Yes. You can include your spouse, de facto partner, and dependent children. They will be granted the same permanent residency rights as you if the visa is approved.

faqs.q: What is the occupation ceiling and how does it affect me?
faqs.a: The occupation ceiling limits how many invitations are issued for each occupation annually. If your occupation hits its ceiling early, you may not receive an invitation, even with a high points score.

blocks.x: The Subclass 491 lets you live, work and study in a designated regional area of Australia for up to 5 years. It is not a permanent visa.
A state or territory must nominate you, or an eligible relative who lives in a designated regional area must sponsor you. That nomination or sponsorship adds 15 points.

An eligible relative is usually a close family member, such as a parent, child, brother, sister, aunt, uncle, niece, nephew, grandparent or first cousin. hero.h1: Employer Sponsored Visas in Australia
intro: An employer sponsored visa lets an Australian business hire a skilled person from overseas, or keep a worker it already employs. Some visas lead to permanent residence. Others are temporary. Which one fits depends on the job, the pay, the location and the person. Our registered migration agents act for workers and for employers, so you get advice that fits both sides of the deal.

sections.name: Who this is for
sections.h2: Are you the worker or the employer?

blocks.x: Most sponsorship cases involve both. The employer sponsors and nominates. The worker applies for the visa. Each visa page below shows what applies to each side.
**Workers and graduates.** You have a job offer and want to know which visa applies, or you hold a 482 and want to reach permanent residence.

**Employers.** You cannot fill a role locally, you have never sponsored before, or you sponsor already and need help with nominations, renewals or compliance. Start with the [Application Process Guide](/employer-sponsored/application-process-guide).
Most employer sponsored visas follow the same three stages. Each stage has its own forms, charges and processing time.

faqs.q: What is an employer sponsored visa?
faqs.a: It is a visa where an Australian business supports your application. The business is approved as a sponsor and nominates your job. You then apply for the visa. Some visas are temporary and some are permanent.

faqs.q: Can I sponsor myself?
faqs.a: No. The sponsor must be a separate, genuine business. If you own the business, special rules apply and the Department looks closely at whether the job is genuine. Speak to an agent before you start.

faqs.q: Who pays for the sponsorship?
faqs.a: The employer pays the sponsorship, nomination and SAF levy costs, and cannot recover them from the worker. The visa application charge can be paid by either side.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the 482 and the 186?
faqs.a: The 482 is a temporary visa, up to four years. The 186 is permanent. Many 482 holders move to a 186 through the Temporary Residence Transition stream. Read the [482 page](/employer-sponsored/sid-visa-482) and the [186 TRT page](/employer-sponsored/ens-186-trt).

faqs.q: Does the employer have to advertise the job first?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Labour market testing applies to some nominations and not others. See the [Position Nomination Process Guide](/employer-sponsored/nomination-process).

faqs.q: Can I change employers on a sponsored visa?
faqs.a: Usually you can, but a new employer must be an approved sponsor and nominate you, and you must stay within the time limits that apply to you. Get advice before you resign.

faqs.q: How long does it take?
faqs.a: It depends on the visa and the Department's workload. The three stages together usually take several months.

faqs.q: Can you guarantee the visa?
faqs.a: No. Only the Department of Home Affairs decides visa applications. We tell you honestly whether your case looks realistic before you spend money.

cta.text: Tell us whether you are the worker or the employer, and what you need. We reply within one business day.

The visa was called the Temporary Skill Shortage (TSS) visa until December 2024. The streams have changed. The old short-term and medium-term streams no longer apply to new applications. intro: A Designated Area Migration Agreement is a deal between the Australian Government and a regional body, such as a state agency or council. sections.name: What a DAMA is
sections.h2: What is a DAMA, in plain English?

items.x: **Endorsement first.** A regional body must endorse your business and the role before you nominate.

intro: The 494 is a five-year visa for skilled workers sponsored by an employer in regional Australia. It has a defined path to permanent residence through the Subclass 191 visa. We help regional employers set up the sponsorship and help workers decide whether the 494 is the right choice over a 482.

blocks.x: The 494 lets a regional business hire a skilled worker from overseas, or from within Australia, for up to five years. The worker must live and work in a regional area for the sponsor. The visa was built to bring skills to places that find it hard to hire.

sections.name: Enquiry form and final CTA
sections.h2: Thinking about sponsoring or working in regional Australia?

faqs.q: What areas count as regional?
faqs.a: In general, areas outside Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane. Boundaries are set by postcode. Use our [Regional Postcode Checker](/postcode-checker).

faqs.q: Do I need state nomination for the 494?
faqs.a: No. The employer nominates you. Some states may support employers separately, which is not the same as state nomination.

faqs.q: Can I change employers?
faqs.a: Only with a new nomination from an approved sponsor in a regional area. Get advice first.

faqs.q: How do I get PR from a 494?
faqs.a: Through the Subclass 191 after meeting the requirements.

faqs.q: Can my family come?
faqs.a: Yes, usually.

faqs.q: What if the employer relocates?
faqs.a: The visa is tied to the sponsor and the region. Speak to us before any change.

faqs.q: What is the salary threshold?
faqs.a: At least the TSMIT and the market rate.

faqs.q: Can I move to Melbourne later?
faqs.a: During the visa, you must stay in the regional area. After PR, you can live anywhere.

cta.text: Tell us the location, the role and your goals. We will tell you whether the 494 is the right visa.

hero.h1: Temporary Work (Short Stay Specialist) Visa (Subclass 400): Requirements and Process
intro: The 400 visa is for a specialist who must do a short, non-ongoing job in Australia. Think of an engineer who must install or repair a machine, or an expert who must run a short project. It does not need the full sponsor and nomination process. It does need a strong case that the work is highly specialised and short. We help businesses and specialists prepare that case.

blocks.x: The 400 lets a person do very short, highly specialised work in Australia without the sponsor and nomination steps used for the 482. The work must be needed for a limited time and must not be a regular job.

faqs.q: Do I need a sponsor for the 400?
faqs.a: There is no formal sponsorship, but an Australian organisation should invite you and support the application.

faqs.q: How long can I stay?
faqs.a: Usually up to three months, and sometimes up to six.

faqs.q: What counts as highly specialised work?
faqs.a: Work that needs rare skills and is limited in time, such as servicing specialised equipment. General skilled work does not count.

blocks.x: The Employer Nomination Scheme (subclass 186) is a permanent visa. It has more than one stream. The Temporary Residence Transition stream is for people who already work in Australia for a sponsor on a temporary skilled visa.

Your employer nominates you for a permanent position. If they are approved and you meet the visa rules, you can be granted permanent residence. You can live and work anywhere in Australia, and you are no longer tied to the sponsor.
**Rule changes:** The time with your sponsor was reduced from three years to two in November 2023. A later change in late 2025 affects which sponsors count.

your employer wants to keep you permanently; and

intro: Most employer sponsored visas need three things in order: an approved sponsor, an approved nomination and a visa application. Each stage has its own forms, fees and timing. This guide shows what happens at each stage, who does the work, and where businesses and workers most often go wrong.

hero.h1: Family and Partner Visas in Australia
intro: Bringing your partner, parents or children to Australia is personal, and the rules are strict. Our registered migration agents explain the visa options, the real costs, how long you may wait and what you promise as a sponsor, before you spend any money.

blocks.x: You may need a family visa if you are:

items.x: an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen who wants your husband, wife or de facto partner to live with you in Australia
engaged and planning to marry in Australia
an adult child who wants your parents to live in Australia
a parent or carer with a child overseas who needs a visa
an applicant with a relative in Australia who may qualify under a relative or carer category

blocks.x: Start with who you want to bring to Australia, then pick the group below. If you are not sure where you fit, [book a consultation](/book-an-appointment). A registered agent will tell you which options exist, and which do not.

A partner visa has two stages. You apply once and pay once. First you receive a temporary visa. About two years after you applied, you provide updated evidence for the permanent visa. The deciding question is where the applicant is when you lodge.

blocks.x: Australia caps the number of parent visas each year. That is why parent visas cost more, wait longer, or both. All permanent parent visas must pass the **Balance of Family test**: at least half of the parent's children must live permanently in Australia, or more of them than in any other single country.

sections.name: What sponsors must know
sections.h2: Being a sponsor: what you are agreeing to

blocks.x: The sponsor is the Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen who supports the application. Sponsors often do not realise what this means until the form is in front of them.

items.x: **You must be approved.** Home Affairs assesses you as well as the applicant, including police checks. Some criminal history, such as family violence offences, can stop a sponsorship.
**There are limits.** A sponsor can usually sponsor only a limited number of partners in a lifetime, and there is normally a gap of five years between sponsorships.

**You give a financial undertaking.** For partner visas the sponsor agrees to support the applicant for a set period. For parent visas an Assurance of Support (a bond and a financial promise) is usually required.
**You cannot just withdraw.** If the relationship ends, the visa process continues in some circumstances. Family violence provisions protect applicants in unsafe relationships.

sections.name: Proving your relationship
sections.h2: The four areas of relationship evidence

blocks.x: Case officers look at four areas to decide if your relationship is genuine and continuing:

items.x: **Financial.** Joint bank accounts, shared bills, shared loans or leases, how you support each other.
**Household.** Where you live, who does what at home, joint address on mail and records.
**Social.** Photos, invitations, travel together, statements from friends and family about your relationship.
**Commitment.** How you speak about the future, how you keep in contact when apart, your plans together.

blocks.x: No single document proves a relationship. We help you present a complete, honest picture, including when your situation is not typical (long distance, cultural marriage, separate addresses for work).

**Government charges.** Home Affairs sets these and changes them, usually each 1 July. A partner visa is one of the most expensive visas to lodge. Check the Department of Home Affairs website for the current charge.

**Other costs.** Budget for health examinations, police certificates, document translations and, for parent visas, private health insurance and the Assurance of Support. Our professional fees are separate and set out in a written agreement.
**Waiting times.** A partner visa decision commonly takes more than a year. Parent visas vary from a few months (870) to many years (103 and 804).
For the two-instalment parent visas, see our [cost for contributory visas page](/family-visa/cost-for-contributory-visas).

faqs.q: How long does a partner visa take?
faqs.a: It depends on whether you apply onshore or offshore and on how complete your evidence is. Many couples wait more than a year for the first stage, then the permanent stage follows about two years after you lodged.

faqs.q: How much does a partner visa cost?
faqs.a: The Department charges a single application fee for both stages, with extra charges for additional applicants. Health checks, police certificates and translations add to the total.

faqs.q: Can I live in Australia while my partner visa is processed?
faqs.a: If you apply onshore on a substantive visa you can usually stay on a bridging visa. If you apply offshore you usually wait overseas.

faqs.q: Which parent visa is fastest?
faqs.a: The Sponsored Parent Temporary visa (870) has the shortest wait but gives no permanent residence. Permanent parent visas take much longer.

faqs.q: Do I need to be an Australian citizen to sponsor?
faqs.a: No. Permanent residents and eligible New Zealand citizens can sponsor, as long as they are approved sponsors.

faqs.q: What happens if my relationship ends?
faqs.a: This depends on the stage and the reason. Special rules apply if there is family violence. Speak to an agent as soon as possible.

faqs.q: Do you guarantee a visa?
faqs.a: No. Only the Department of Home Affairs decides. We help you prepare the strongest honest application.

faqs.q: Can I switch from a visitor visa to a partner visa?
faqs.a: Often yes, but it depends on the conditions on your current visa. We check this at your consultation.

sections.name: What the 309 is and who it suits

blocks.x: The Subclass 309 is the first stage of the offshore partner visa. You apply for the 309 and 100 together in one application. If the Department approves it, you get the 309 first. This lets you enter Australia and live with your partner. Around two years after you lodged, the Department assesses you for the permanent 100.
It suits you if:

items.x: you are married to, or in a de facto relationship with, an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible NZ citizen
you are outside Australia
you are happy to wait overseas, or can visit Australia on a visitor visa while you wait

sections.name: Is this the right visa for you?

blocks.x: Tick the boxes that apply.

items.x: I am married, or I have lived with my partner for at least 12 months (or can register our relationship).
I am outside Australia and will be when the visa is decided
My sponsor is an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible NZ citizen who is willing to sponsor me
We can show our relationship is genuine and ongoing
We can accept a wait of well over a year for stage 1

blocks.x: **309 or 820?** If you are in Australia on a [substantive visa, the Subclass 820](/family-visa/partner-provisional-visa-subclass-820) may be possible, which lets you stay here on a bridging visa while you wait. If you are overseas, the 309 is the correct route. Some people apply onshore to avoid the long wait overseas, but only if they genuinely qualify. We check this at the start.
**The applicant must:**

items.x: be the spouse or de facto partner of the sponsor
be outside Australia when applying and when the visa is decided
meet health and character requirements, including police certificates from countries where you lived for 12 months or more in the last 10 years
meet Australian values requirements and sign the Australian values statement
have no debts to the Australian Government, or an arrangement in place

blocks.x: **The relationship must be:**

items.x: genuine and continuing
to the exclusion of all others
for de facto couples, a relationship of at least 12 months, unless the relationship was registered or a compelling reason applies

blocks.x: **The sponsor must:**

items.x: be 18 or over and an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible NZ citizen
be approved as a sponsor, including a police check
meet any sponsorship limits (see the next section)

blocks.x: Many sponsors do not realise they are making a legal promise. For a partner visa:

items.x: **Financial support.** The sponsor undertakes to support the applicant for a set time so they do not need certain social security payments.
**Accommodation help.** The sponsor undertakes to help with accommodation for a limited period.
**Character checks.** Serious criminal history, including some family violence offences, can lead to the sponsorship being refused.

**Sponsorship limits.** A sponsor can normally sponsor only a limited number of partners over a lifetime and usually must wait five years between sponsorships. A sponsor who arrived as a partner visa applicant can also face restrictions.

blocks.x: If you have sponsored before, tell us at your first meeting. This is one of the most common reasons an application is refused or delayed.

blocks.x: The government charge is paid once and covers both stages. You are not charged again for the permanent 100 in most cases.
Government charges usually change on 1 July. Always check the current amount on the Home Affairs website before you lodge.

The Department publishes processing times for partner visas. Times change with demand and the number of applications lodged. The date of your application, how complete your evidence is and any health or character checks all affect your timeline.
Plan this way:

items.x: **Stage 1 (309).** Expect many months, often more than a year. A complete application with strong evidence helps avoid delays.
**Stage 2 (100).** The Department assesses you for the permanent visa from about two years after you lodged.

**While you wait.** You usually wait outside Australia. You may be able to visit on a visitor visa, but visitor visa conditions apply and you should not stay beyond your permitted time. See our [visitor visa page](/visitor-visa).
**Check eligibility.** Book a consultation. We assess your relationship, your sponsor's history and any risks.
**Sponsor lodges the sponsorship form.** The Australian sponsor completes and lodges this with the visa application.
**Gather evidence.** Four areas: financial, household, social, commitment. We list what is relevant to you.
**Lodge online.** Your application is lodged through ImmiAccount, with documents uploaded.
**Health and police checks.** You attend a panel doctor and obtain police certificates, when asked.
**Respond to requests.** The Department may ask for more evidence or an interview.
**Decision and grant.** If approved, you receive your 309 and can travel to Australia.
**Stage 2.** Around two years after lodging, you provide fresh [evidence for the Subclass 100](/family-visa/partner-permanent-visa-subclass-100).

sections.name: Common mistakes and refusal risks
sections.h2: Mistakes that cause delays or refusals

items.x: **Thin evidence for a long-distance relationship.** Show visits, calls and shared plans. Not just photos.
**Inconsistent dates.** Different dates for when you met or began living together across forms.
**Overlooking prior relationships.** Not disclosing an earlier relationship or sponsorship.
**Relying on the marriage certificate alone.** Marriage is not enough. The Department tests whether the relationship is genuine.
**Ignoring sponsor history.** A sponsor with a relevant criminal history or earlier sponsorships may be refused.
**Late responses.** Missing a deadline for a request for information.

blocks.x: If your application is refused, you may have review rights. See our [visa refusal page](/appeals/visa-refusal).

sections.name: Next step
sections.h2: After the 309: your path to permanent residence

blocks.x: Your [309 leads to the Subclass 100](/family-visa/partner-permanent-visa-subclass-100). The Department will ask you for updated evidence and often a fresh sponsor statement. Citizenship is a later step once you meet the residence rule. See our [citizenship page](/citizenship).

sections.name: Can I work or study on the 309?
sections.h2: Can I work or study on the 309?

blocks.x: Yes. You have full work and study rights once the 309 is granted. Medicare access follows the grant too. Before the grant, you usually wait outside Australia. You may visit on a visitor visa, but its conditions apply and you must not stay beyond your permitted time. See our [visitor visa page](/visitor-visa).

blocks.label: Note
blocks.x: This page is general information, not legal advice. A registered migration agent must assess your case. The Department of Home Affairs makes all visa decisions.

The 309 is for applicants who are outside Australia and already married or in a de facto relationship. If your partner is in Australia, look at the 820. If you are engaged and not yet married, look at the 300.
Not sure which applies? [Book a consultation](/book-an-appointment) and a registered agent will check where you are, your visa conditions and your relationship history.

faqs.q: Can I work in Australia on a 309 visa?
faqs.a: Yes. Once granted, the 309 gives full work and study rights.

faqs.q: Can I apply for the 309 if I am in Australia?
faqs.a: No. You must be outside Australia when you apply. If you are in Australia, the 820 may apply. See the [820 page](/family-visa/partner-provisional-visa-subclass-820).

faqs.q: Can my partner visit me while I wait?
faqs.a: You may be able to visit on a visitor visa. Check the conditions, because some visitor visas do not let you stay long.

faqs.q: What if we are not married?
faqs.a: De facto partners can apply, but usually must show 12 months together unless the relationship is registered or another exception applies.

faqs.q: Do we need to live together?
faqs.a: Not always, for example for work or cultural reasons, but you must show you are committed to a shared life.

faqs.q: What if our relationship ends before the 100 is decided?
faqs.a: Special rules apply, including for family violence. Talk to a registered migration agent immediately.

faqs.q: How much will I pay in total?
faqs.a: Add the government charge, health checks, police certificates, translations and professional fees.

faqs.q: Can you guarantee a 309 visa?
faqs.a: No. Only the Department of Home Affairs decides. We help you prepare the strongest honest application.

blocks.x: The Subclass 100 is the permanent partner visa for applicants who applied outside Australia. It is the second half of the application you lodged for the 309. The Department decides on the 100 after a fixed period and wants to know if the relationship is still genuine and ongoing.
If your relationship has been long, the Department may decide on the 100 sooner.

items.x: Usually from about two years after you lodged the application.
Sooner if your relationship was long when you applied.
Later if your application was delayed, or if the Department needs further checks.

blocks.x: Do not wait until you are asked. Start collecting evidence from the day your 309 is granted. A folder you build over time is far easier to complete than a scramble in month 22.

items.x: You still hold the 309 (or your application is being assessed with it).
You and your sponsor are still in a genuine, continuing relationship, or you meet a family violence provision.
You meet health and character requirements again where needed.
The sponsor is still eligible to sponsor.
You have no unpaid debts to the Australian Government.

items.x: **Receive the notice.** The Department contacts you when stage 2 is due.
**Book a review.** We check what is needed and look for gaps.
**Update your evidence.** Cover the whole period since the 309 was granted.
**Update sponsor information.** Your sponsor provides statements and, if required, police checks.
**Upload and respond.** Provide everything in your ImmiAccount by the date given.
**Decision.** If approved, you become a permanent resident.

sections.name: If the relationship has changed
sections.h2: If you separate before the 100 is decided

blocks.x: A separation does not always end your visa path. If the relationship ended because of family violence, special provisions may allow you to keep going. In other cases the rules are strict. If your relationship has broken down, speak to a registered migration agent straight away. We will explain your options, privately and without judgement.
If you need urgent help with family violence, contact 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732).

items.x: Permanent residence: you can live, work and study in Australia without time limit.
Medicare access.
Sponsorship rights for some relatives.
Citizenship pathway after you meet the residence requirements. See our [citizenship page](/citizenship).
Travel: if you leave and your travel facility lapses, you may need a Resident Return Visa. See [Resident Return visas](/bridging-return-visas/resident-return-visa-155-157).

blocks.x: The 100 is the permanent stage for people who applied from outside Australia and hold a 309. If you applied inside Australia, your permanent stage is the 801.
Not sure which applies? [Book a consultation](/book-an-appointment) and a registered agent will check where you are, your visa conditions and your relationship history.

blocks.label: Note
blocks.x: This page is general information, not legal advice. A registered migration agent must assess your case. The Department of Home Affairs makes all visa decisions.

faqs.q: Do I need to apply for the 100 myself?
faqs.a: In most cases you do not lodge a separate form. The Department contacts you for evidence.

faqs.q: What if I do not hear from the Department after two years?
faqs.a: Check your ImmiAccount and contact us. Do not assume the visa is automatic.

faqs.q: Can I leave Australia while the 100 is pending?
faqs.a: Usually yes on the 309, but check your visa conditions first.

faqs.q: What if we separated?
faqs.a: Get advice right away.

faqs.q: Can I work and use Medicare on a 309?
faqs.a: Yes, in most cases. The permanent 100 continues this.

faqs.q: Is the 100 the same as the 801?
faqs.a: They are the same permanent stage. The 100 follows the offshore 309. The 801 follows the onshore 820.

faqs.q: Does the 100 expire?
faqs.a: The visa is permanent. Your travel facility may lapse, so check before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I work while my 820 is processed?
faqs.a: Usually yes on your bridging visa, but conditions vary. We check your visa at the first meeting.

faqs.q: Can I leave Australia while waiting?
faqs.a: Only with a Bridging Visa B or similar. Leaving without one can mean you cannot come back.

faqs.q: What is condition 8503?
faqs.a: A condition on some visas that says you cannot apply for another visa in Australia. A waiver is possible in limited cases.

faqs.q: Do I need to be married?
faqs.a: No. De facto partners can apply, usually showing 12 months together or a registered relationship.

faqs.q: Can I apply on a visitor visa?
faqs.a: Sometimes. It depends on the visa conditions.

faqs.q: Is the 820 the same as the 309?
faqs.a: They are similar visas for different locations. See [309](/family-visa/partner-provisional-visa-subclass-309).

faqs.a: Special rules apply, including for family violence. Talk to us quickly.

faqs.q: Can you guarantee the 820?

head: Fact
Detail
rows: A parent outside Australia, with a child settled in Australia as sponsor
Check the Department of Home Affairs website for the current figure.

blocks.x: The 143 gives a parent permanent residence in Australia. It is "contributory" because the parent pays a much larger second charge toward their expected healthcare and support costs. In return the queue is shorter than [for the lower-fee Subclass 103](/family-visa/parent-visa-subclass-103). It is still a capped visa, so there is a queue.
It suits families who:

items.x: want their parents to live permanently in Australia
can afford the higher charges and the Assurance of Support
accept that the process takes years, not months

blocks.x: **Balance of Family test:** at least half of the parent's children must live permanently in Australia, or more of the parent's children must live permanently in Australia than in any other single country. Children means all biological, adopted and step-children, including those who have passed away or lost contact.
**Sponsor:** a child (or a spouse of the child) who is an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible NZ citizen, usually settled in Australia for at least two years.

sections.h2: Sponsor and Assurance of Support: what you are signing

items.x: **Sponsor.** The child sponsors the parent and may be assessed on character.
**Assurance of Support (AoS).** An assurer promises to repay certain social security payments the parent receives during the AoS period. A bond is lodged with Services Australia.
**The assurer is legally responsible.** This is a financial commitment, not a formality. Read it carefully and take advice.
**Income test.** The assurer must show enough income.

**Who pays.** The parent, the sponsor and the assurer may all contribute. Make sure everyone agrees before lodging. If you withdraw after lodging, refunds are limited.
Home Affairs publishes a processing time for contributory parent visas. It is measured in years.
Why so long? The Government sets a yearly cap on parent visas as part of the Migration Program planning levels, and applications are processed in the order lodged. The cap is far lower than demand.

hero.h1: Parent Visa (Subclass 103): Requirements, Fees and the Real Wait
intro: Understand the lower-cost permanent parent visa, and why the wait is the main thing to plan around.

head: Fact
Detail
rows: Check the Department of Home Affairs website for the current figure.

blocks.x: The 103 is the lower-cost permanent parent visa for parents outside Australia. The government charge is far lower than for the contributory 143. The trade-off is a queue that is measured in decades, because the number of visas each year is very small compared with the number of applicants.
For many families it is a long-term plan, not a near-term solution.

blocks.x: **Be honest with yourself.** If your parents need to be in Australia within a few years, the 103 is unlikely to deliver that. Families sometimes lodge a 103 to hold a place in the queue while using [visitor visas or the 870](/family-visa/sponsored-parent-temporary-visa-subclass-870) for time together. We discuss this openly.

blocks.x: Processing is by queue. Only a small number of visas are granted each year.

items.x: If you lodge today, your parent may be much older at grant than now.
Health requirements are assessed late. A condition that appears during the wait can be a barrier. Ask us about health waiver rules.
Your family may change. The Balance of Family test is assessed at decision, not at lodgement.
In the meantime, your parent may visit on a visitor visa. See [visitor visas](/visitor-visa).
**Consultation.** We test the Balance of Family and compare options.
**Lodge.** Submit the application and pay the charge.

faqs.q: How long is the wait for a 103?
faqs.a: Extremely long.

faqs.q: Why is it so low cost?
faqs.a: Because the government expects the parent to rely more on public systems. That is why the contributory visa costs more.

faqs.q: Can I apply for a 103 and a 143 together?
faqs.a: Usually no. Speak to us about the correct approach.

faqs.q: What is the Balance of Family test?

faqs.q: Can my parent visit while waiting?
faqs.a: Often yes, on a visitor visa, subject to its conditions.

faqs.q: Does my parent need to be a certain age?
faqs.a: Not for the offshore 103. The onshore 804 requires age pension age.

faqs.q: Do I get a refund if I withdraw?

sections.name: What the Child visa (subclass 101) is, and who it suits

blocks.x: The subclass 101 is a permanent visa. It lets a child who lives overseas move to Australia and stay with a parent who is an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen. Once granted, the child can live, study and work in Australia and use Medicare.
**It suits you if:**

items.x: your child lives overseas and you want them to join you in Australia for good
your child was born overseas and you became a permanent resident or citizen after the birth
you recently had a child overseas with a new partner and want to bring them to Australia
you are an Australian parent whose stepchild lives overseas and you want to sponsor them

blocks.x: **It does not suit you if** your child is already in Australia. In that case the onshore Child visa may apply. See our [page on the Child Visa Subclass 802](/family-visa/child-visa-subclass-802).

sections.name: After the grant
sections.h2: What happens once your child arrives?

blocks.x: The 101 is a permanent visa, so there is no "next visa" to apply for. A child with a permanent visa can apply for Australian citizenship once they meet the residence and other requirements. See [Australian Citizenship](/citizenship).
Keep the visa grant notice and passport safe. If you plan overseas travel after arrival, check the travel facility conditions on the visa.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the Child visa 101 and 802?
faqs.a: The 101 is for a child who is outside Australia at the time of application and decision. The 802 is for a child who is in Australia.

faqs.q: Can I include my other children?
faqs.a: Possibly, if they are included members of the family unit and meet the requirements. A separate application may be needed for some children. Book a consultation so we can check.

faqs.q: Does my child need a medical?
faqs.a: Yes. Health examinations are part of the process. The Department will tell you how and when to arrange them.

faqs.q: Can my child work or study in Australia?
faqs.a: Yes. A permanent resident child can attend school and work, subject to age and law.

faqs.q: What if the other parent lives overseas and does not agree?
faqs.a: The Department may need a court order or other proof. This is a legal matter. A registered agent can explain the general steps and refer you to a family lawyer if needed.

faqs.q: Do I need a migration agent?
faqs.a: No, but mistakes can cause delay or refusal. An agent helps you prepare the evidence and respond to the Department.

faqs.q: Can a step-parent sponsor?
faqs.a: Often yes, if the step-parent is an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen and the relationship meets the rules.

faqs.q: How much will it cost?
faqs.a: The government charge changes., and ask us for a written quote.

faqs.q: Can you guarantee the visa?
faqs.a: No. Only the Department of Home Affairs decides. We tell you honestly whether the case looks strong.

intro: Your child is here with you, but they do not have a permanent visa. The Child visa (subclass 802) is the onshore route to permanent residence for a child of an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen. We check your child's current visa, explain the steps and help you lodge with the right evidence.

sections.name: What the 802 is and who it suits

blocks.x: The subclass 802 is a permanent visa for a child who is already in Australia. It is the same type of visa as the 101, but the child applies from inside the country. When it is granted, the child can live in Australia permanently, study, work and use Medicare.
**It often suits:**

items.x: a child who arrived on a visitor or student visa and whose parent has since become a permanent resident or citizen
a child of a parent who has just been granted a partner or skilled visa
a child born in Australia who did not automatically become a citizen
a stepchild living in Australia with a step-parent who is an Australian citizen or permanent resident

Meets age and dependency rules.
Passes health and character checks.

sections.name: Processing times and your child's visa status
sections.h2: How long does it take, and can my child stay meanwhile?

blocks.x: Processing times vary and can be long.

When you lodge a valid 802 application, your child may be given a bridging visa. This lets them stay lawfully while waiting. A bridging visa can have conditions. For example, travel can be limited, so do not book overseas travel without advice. See [Bridging Visa A (010)](/bridging-return-visas/bridging-visa-a-010).

items.x: **Check the child's current visa.** Look at the expiry date and conditions.
**Confirm sponsor eligibility.** Gather citizenship or permanent residence proof.
**Collect evidence.** Birth certificate, passports and consent documents.
**Lodge through ImmiAccount.** Attach documents and pay the charge.
**Bridging visa check.** Confirm a bridging visa is in place before the old visa ends.
**Health and police checks.** Arrange when the Department asks.
**Respond to requests.** Reply on time.
**Decision.** If granted, update records with school and Medicare.
Child's passport and current visa grant
Birth certificate showing parents
Sponsor's proof of citizenship or permanent residence
Proof of relationship to a step-parent, if relevant
Consent from the other parent or court order, if relevant

Evidence of residence in Australia (school letters, Medicare card)
Health and police documents when requested
Certified translations
**Visa ends before the application is lodged.** An unlawful child cannot apply in many cases.
**A condition blocks an onshore application.** Check conditions before you pay.
**The child travels while on a bridging visa.** Some bridging visas do not allow return.
**Birth citizenship assumptions.** A child born in Australia is a citizen only in some circumstances. Do not assume.
**Missing consent from a parent.** This can stall the case.
**Late lodging.** Age rules are tested at application.

blocks.x: If the application is refused, you may have review rights. See [Appeals](/appeals).

We check your child's current visa and its conditions, confirm the sponsor's status, list the documents you need and lodge the application. Bring your child's visa grant, passports and any court orders to your first appointment in Melbourne (Collins St) or Adelaide (Gawler Pl), or speak to us by phone or video.

Because the 802 is permanent, no further visa is needed. After meeting the residence and other rules, the child [may apply for Australian citizenship](/citizenship). A child under 18 may qualify sooner than an adult.

faqs.q: Can my child stay in Australia while the 802 is processed?
faqs.a: Often, yes, on a bridging visa. The details depend on their current visa. We check this at the start.

faqs.q: What if my child's visa expires before I lodge?
faqs.a: This can create serious problems. Contact us quickly. If time is short, tell us at the start of the call.

faqs.q: Can I apply for the 802 and the 101 at the same time?
faqs.a: No. The child's location decides which visa applies.

faqs.q: Can my child's sibling be included?
faqs.a: Each child is usually assessed separately, and sibling rules depend on circumstances. We can check.

faqs.q: Does my child need a medical?
faqs.a: Yes, when the Department asks.

faqs.q: Can an adult child (18 to 24) apply?
faqs.a: Maybe, if still dependent. Evidence is key.

faqs.q: Is the 802 faster than the 101?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Compare current published times.

faqs.q: Can you guarantee a grant?
faqs.a: No. Only the Department decides.

intro: Contributory parent visas are faster than other parent visas, but they cost much more. The government charge is paid in two parts, and there are other costs on top. This page sets out what you are likely to pay, so you can plan before you decide.

sections.h2: What the costs are made of

blocks.x: A contributory parent visa has a government charge, usually paid in two parts, plus other costs such as health checks, assurance of support and professional fees. Check the Department of Home Affairs website for the current charge.

items.x: **Assurance of support.** A sponsor, usually your child, may need to provide an assurance of support and a bond for several years.
**Health examinations.** Panel doctor fees vary by country and age.
**Health insurance.** Cover for the visa holder may be needed.
**Police certificates and translations.** Fees vary by country.
**Travel and living costs.** Plan for flights, housing and daily costs.
**Professional fees.** See our professional fees below.

sections.name: Contributory vs non-contributory
sections.h2: Why are contributory visas more expensive?

blocks.x: Contributory visas ask the applicant to contribute to the cost of health and welfare services, so the government charge is higher. In return, the waiting time is usually shorter. Non-contributory parent visas such [as the Parent Visa 103](/family-visa/parent-visa-subclass-103) and [Aged Parent Visa 804](/family-visa/aged-parent-visa-subclass-804) cost less in government charges but have much longer waits.
The right choice depends on your parent's age, health, your finances and how long your family can wait.

blocks.x: The temporary contributory visas allow a parent to stay in Australia for a limited period while the permanent application is being considered. Costs can add up if you apply for both stages. Ask us to add the stages together for your case. See also [Sponsored Parent Temporary Visa 870](/family-visa/sponsored-parent-temporary-visa-subclass-870) as a shorter option.

**Check payment methods.** Pay charges only through the Department's official channels.
**Keep records.** Keep receipts and the application ID.

hero.h1: Australian Visitor Visa Help: Find the Right Visa for Your Trip
intro: Visiting Australia, or inviting someone to visit you? The right visa depends on your passport, where you are when you apply, why you are travelling and how long you want to stay. Our registered migration agents help you choose the correct visa, prepare your evidence and avoid the mistakes that lead to refusals.

sections.name: What is your trip about?
sections.h2: Which visa is right for you?

blocks.x: Start with your reason for travelling. Then check your passport and where you will be when you apply. Fees, processing times and eligible passports change, so check the Department of Home Affairs website before you lodge.

Read
rows: Holiday, sightsee or visit friends on any passport
Have a parent, sibling or other relative visit you
Attend meetings, a conference or a trade fair
[Visitor visa 600](/visitor-visa/visitor-visa-600), or the ETA or eVisitor if your passport is eligible

Make a short trip on an eligible European passport
Travel and work for up to 12 months while you are young (417 countries)
Travel and work for up to 12 months while you are young (462 countries)
Stay longer while you are in Australia
Come back for another visit or a longer stay from overseas

blocks.x: An ETA or eVisitor covers stays of up to 3 months at a time. A visitor visa (600) can be granted for longer. A visitor visa is not extended. You usually apply for a new one.

sections.name: What decides a visitor visa
sections.h2: The test behind every visitor visa

blocks.x: The Department of Home Affairs must be satisfied that you intend to visit Australia temporarily and then leave. This is the genuine temporary stay test in clause 600.211 of Schedule 2 to the Migration Regulations. The decision maker looks at your whole situation. No single document guarantees a grant.

head: What they look at
Evidence that helps
rows: Employer letter with approved leave and return date, recent payslips and tax returns, business registration if self-employed, proof of study
Recent bank statements showing steady funds, an explanation for any large or recent deposits, evidence of assets
Close family who stay at home, a travel history that shows you followed visa conditions

sections.name: Conditions to know
sections.h2: Visa conditions that catch visitors out

items.x: **Condition 8101 (no work).** You cannot work in Australia on a standard visitor visa.
**Condition 8201 (study limit).** Study is limited to 3 months.
**Condition 8503 (no further stay).** You cannot apply for most other visas while you are in Australia. A waiver is only given in limited, compelling cases.
**Condition 8558 (stay limit).** You cannot stay more than 12 months in any 18-month period.

blocks.x: Breaking a condition can lead to cancellation and make later visa applications harder. Check your grant letter for the conditions on your visa.

sections.name: Why visitor visas get refused
sections.h2: Common reasons visitor visas are refused

items.x: Weak ties to home, such as no job, no leave approval or no close family there.
Savings that do not match the trip, or unexplained deposits.
A vague itinerary, or one that does not match the stated purpose.
A history of overstays, refusals or breaches that was not explained.
A sponsor or host who has not shown their own status or relationship.
Answers on the form that do not match your documents.

blocks.x: A refusal stays on your record and is asked about in later applications. If you were refused, read our [visa refusal page](/appeals/visa-refusal) before you reapply. Our registered migration agents review your evidence, tell you honestly if it is thin and prepare a cover submission that addresses the genuine temporary stay test. We cannot guarantee any visa outcome.

faqs.q: Which visa do I need to visit Australia?
faqs.a: It depends on your passport and purpose. Some passport holders can use an ETA (601) or eVisitor (651). Others apply for a visitor visa (600). Young people from eligible countries may use a working holiday or work and holiday visa.

faqs.q: What is the difference between ETA 601 and eVisitor 651?
faqs.a: Both are quick online authorities for short visits. The ETA is for eligible non-European passports and is applied for by app, with a service charge. The eVisitor is free and for eligible European passports.

faqs.q: How long can I stay on a visitor visa?
faqs.a: It depends on the visa granted. ETA and eVisitor allow up to 3 months per visit. A 600 is usually granted for 3, 6 or 12 months. Condition 8558 may also limit total time.

faqs.q: Can I work on a visitor visa?
faqs.a: No. Visitor visas carry condition 8101. Business visitors can attend meetings and conferences, but they cannot do productive work or sell services to the public.

faqs.q: Can my parents visit me in Melbourne?
faqs.a: Yes, usually on a visitor visa (600). If you are an Australian citizen or permanent resident, you may sponsor them under the Sponsored Family stream. Our Sponsored Family guide explains what you need.

faqs.q: Can I extend my visitor visa?
faqs.a: Not in the usual sense. You apply for a new visitor visa before your current one ends, and condition 8503 may stop you. See our onshore visitor visa extension page.

faqs.q: How long does a visitor visa take?
faqs.a: Processing times change often. Check the Department's current global processing times before you plan.

faqs.q: Why was my visitor visa refused?
faqs.a: The most common reason is that the Department was not satisfied you would leave Australia. Book a consultation so we can read your refusal letter and explain your options.

faqs.q: Does each family member need their own application?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Each traveller, including children, needs their own visa or authority. Check the Department of Home Affairs website for how to apply for children, or ask us.

cta.title: Not sure which visa fits your trip?
cta.text: Tell us your passport, plans and any past visa history. We will tell you the right visa and what evidence you need.

faqs.q: How long can I stay on a visitor visa (600)?
faqs.a: Stay periods are set when the visa is granted, commonly 3, 6 or 12 months. Condition 8558 also limits your total time in Australia. Check your grant letter.

faqs.q: Can I work or study on a 600?
faqs.a: No work is allowed. Study is limited to 3 months. If you want to work or study longer, you need a different visa.

faqs.q: How much money do I need to show?
faqs.a: There is no fixed amount. The Department looks at whether your funds are reasonable for your trip. We help you present your funds clearly.

faqs.q: Do I need a letter of invitation?
faqs.a: It is not always needed for the Tourist stream, but it helps when you are staying with someone. The Sponsored Family stream requires sponsor details.

faqs.q: Can I apply for a 600 if I was refused before?
faqs.a: Often yes, but you must declare it. We review your refusal letter and explain what has changed before you reapply.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the 600 and an ETA?
faqs.a: The ETA is faster and only for eligible passports and short stays. The 600 is for everyone else and for longer stays.

faqs.q: Can I extend a visitor visa while I am in Australia?
faqs.a: Not by simply extending. You generally apply for a new visitor visa before your current visa ends, and condition 8503 may apply. Our [onshore extension page](/visitor-visa/onshore-visitor-visa-extension) explains how.

faqs.q: Will a visitor visa lead to permanent residence?
faqs.a: No. It is a temporary visa. Different visas are needed to live in Australia long term.

faqs.q: Can my family travel with me?
faqs.a: Each traveller generally needs their own visa application. Check the Department of Home Affairs website for how family members apply together, or ask us.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the 462 and the 417?
faqs.a: Both let young people work and holiday for up to 12 months. The 417 is for a different list of countries and has simpler requirements. The 462 often needs English, education and sometimes a government letter.

faqs.q: What is the age limit for the 462?
faqs.a: For most countries you must be 18 to 30 when you lodge. If you are over the limit on that day, the application is invalid.

faqs.q: Can I bring my partner?
faqs.a: Only if they apply for their own visa. You cannot bring dependent children on this visa.

faqs.q: Can I get a second year?

faqs.q: Can I study on a 462?

faqs.q: Can I extend a 462 beyond 12 months?
faqs.a: You cannot simply extend it. Eligible holders may apply for a second or third visa if they meet the rules.

faqs.q: Does the 462 lead to permanent residence?

intro: The ETA is a quick, electronic permission to visit Australia. If your passport is eligible, you apply by app, usually in minutes, and your authority is linked to your passport. It suits short trips for tourism or business. If your passport is not eligible, or your plans do not fit, you need a visitor visa (600) instead.

The ETA is only for short visits. If you want to stay longer than 3 months in one go, you need a visitor visa (600).

faqs.q: Can I extend my visitor visa in Australia?
faqs.a: Not directly. You apply for a new visitor visa before your current visa ends. Condition 8503 may stop you.

faqs.q: What is condition 8503?
faqs.a: A "no further stay" condition. It generally stops you applying for most visas in Australia. A waiver may be possible in limited cases.

faqs.q: How late can I apply?
faqs.a: You must lodge before your current visa expires. Do not wait for the last week.

faqs.q: Can I work while I wait?
faqs.a: No. Working breaches visitor visa conditions.

faqs.q: What is a bridging visa?
faqs.a: A short-term visa that lets you stay lawfully while an application is decided. See our Bridging Visa A page.

faqs.q: Can I travel while on a bridging visa?
faqs.a: Generally not without a travel permission. If you leave, you may not be able to return.

faqs.q: What happens if I overstay?
faqs.a: You become unlawful. This can lead to removal and a ban on returning. Seek advice immediately.

blocks.x: The 188 was a provisional visa for business owners, investors and entrepreneurs. intro: A refusal or cancellation letter is stressful, and the clock is already running. Review deadlines are short and are set out in your decision letter. Find the date, then call us today. A registered migration agent will read your letter and explain your options in plain English.

sections.name: Deadlines at a glance
sections.h2: The deadline is in your decision letter. Find it first.

items.x: **Check the letter.** It says whether you can ask for review, who can review the decision and how long you have.
**The clock may already be running.** Time is counted from when you are taken to have received the notice, not from when you read it.

**Different decisions have different limits.** Refusals, cancellations, decisions made in immigration detention and court review each have their own time limit. Your letter, or an agent, can tell you which applies to you.
**Do not assume a late application will be accepted.** Call us as soon as you have the letter.

**Keep every letter and email** from the Department of Home Affairs. Do not ignore anything.
**Check your visa status.** Look at your visa expiry, any bridging visa and your work or study conditions. Do not travel, sign anything or change your plans before you speak to an agent.
**Gather your paperwork.** Decision letter, copy of your application, passport pages, evidence you sent and emails from the Department.
**Do not rely on social media advice.** Forum answers are often out of date or wrong for your visa type.

faqs.q: What is the ART?
faqs.a: The Administrative Review Tribunal reviews many migration decisions. It replaced the Administrative Appeals Tribunal (AAT) in October 2024. It is independent of the Department of Home Affairs.

faqs.q: Can I stay in Australia while the review is on?
faqs.a: It depends on your visa and any bridging visa you hold. Your status can change quickly, so check with an agent first.

faqs.q: My letter is already a few weeks old. Is it too late?
faqs.a: Maybe not, but do not guess. Call us today so we can count your deadline.

faqs.q: What if I cannot go to the ART?
faqs.a: Other options may exist, such as a new application, a Federal Circuit and Family Court case on legal error, or a request for Ministerial Intervention. Each has strict limits.

faqs.q: Can you guarantee a successful review?
faqs.a: No. Reviews are decided independently. We assess your case honestly and prepare it carefully.

faqs.q: How much does a review cost?
faqs.a: The ART charges an application fee and our fees depend on your case.

faqs.q: How long do I have to apply for review?
faqs.a: It depends on the decision and where you are. Your decision letter states the time limit, and some limits are only days. Call us as soon as you receive the letter.

faqs.q: Can I visit you in Melbourne or Adelaide?
faqs.a: Yes. [Book an appointment](/book-an-appointment) or call +61 3 9602 1330. We also work by phone and video.

hero.h1: Federal Court Visa Appeals: Challenging a Legal Error
intro: A court cannot just re-decide your visa. It can check whether the decision-maker made a legal error. If you think the ART or the Department got the law wrong, the time limit to go to court is very short. Call us now so we can count it.

items.x: **Court time limits are short.** Check the decision and any notice of it for the date.
Do not wait for further paperwork before you call.
Do not assume a late application will be accepted.
**Call us on +61 3 9602 1330.** We will count your deadline.
Find the date of the ART decision and write it down.
Save the full decision and written reasons.
Do not file anything yourself until you know your grounds.
Check your visa or bridging visa and any departure date.
We will assess whether there is an arguable legal error, or whether a different path is better.

sections.name: What a court can and cannot do
sections.h2: What a court can and cannot do

items.x: **Can:** examine whether the decision followed the law and a fair process. Examples may include ignoring a key claim, applying the wrong test or breaching procedural fairness.

faqs.q: What is a bridging visa?
faqs.a: A bridging visa is a temporary visa that lets you stay in Australia lawfully while the Department decides another visa application or while a review is in progress. It is not a visa you apply to stay on forever.

faqs.q: Do I need to apply for a Bridging Visa A?
faqs.a: Usually not. In most cases it is granted automatically when you lodge a valid substantive visa application in Australia while holding a substantive visa. Read the [Bridging Visa A page](/bridging-return-visas/bridging-visa-a-010) for the details.

faqs.q: Can I travel overseas on a bridging visa?
faqs.a: Not on a Bridging Visa A, B or C unless you hold a Bridging Visa B or a travel facility. Leaving Australia without the right visa can end your bridging visa and your right to return. Get advice before you book a flight.

faqs.q: Can I work on a bridging visa?
faqs.a: It depends on the visa and its conditions. Bridging Visa A usually carries the same work and study conditions as your previous visa. Bridging Visa C and E often limit work. Check your visa grant notice.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Bridging Visa A and Bridging Visa C?
faqs.a: You get a Bridging Visa A when you apply while your last visa is still valid. You get a Bridging Visa C when you apply after it has ended. The work, study and travel consequences are different.

faqs.q: What is a Resident Return visa?
faqs.a: It is a visa for permanent residents who want to return to Australia after the travel facility on their permanent visa has ended. See the [Resident Return page](/bridging-return-visas/resident-return-visa-155-157).

faqs.q: My visa was cancelled. What can I do?
faqs.a: You may have review rights with strict deadlines. Contact us straight away. See [Visa Cancellation](/appeals/visa-cancellation).

faqs.q: Do you guarantee a bridging visa?
faqs.a: No. Only the Department of Home Affairs decides. We tell you honestly what is realistic before you spend money.

cta.text: Tell us your current visa and your dates. We will explain what you can and cannot do next.

items.x: **No automatic PR.** Graduating does not guarantee permanent residency. Skilled visas depend on your occupation, skills assessment, points and invitation or nomination.
**Genuine Student scrutiny.** The Department looks at whether your course is a logical step from your past study and work, and whether you intend to study.
**Costs are real.** Tuition, living costs, health cover and the visa charge must be planned. Work income should help with living costs, not be your plan for paying tuition.
**Changing provider early.** In the first six months of your main course you may need a release letter from your provider.
**Rules change.** Student visa settings have changed often in recent years, including fees, funds and who can apply from inside Australia.

**Funds.** You show you can pay for tuition, living costs and travel for yourself and any family members. The required amount has risen in recent years. faqs.q: What is the Subclass 500 student visa?
faqs.a: It lets you stay in Australia to study a full-time CRICOS-registered course. You need a Confirmation of Enrolment, health cover, English, funds and to meet the Genuine Student requirement.

faqs.q: Can I work on a student visa?
faqs.a: Yes, within limits. During your course you can work up to a set number of hours each fortnight, and more in official course breaks. Work is meant to support living costs.

faqs.q: Will studying in Australia get me PR?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Some graduates may become eligible for a graduate visa or a skilled visa. This depends on your occupation, skills assessment, points and current rules. A registered agent can check your case.

faqs.q: How much money do I need to show?
faqs.a: You need to show funds for tuition, living costs and travel. The living-cost figure changes. Try our financial calculator for an estimate.

faqs.q: Can I change my course after I arrive?
faqs.a: Often yes, but the rules depend on the level of the new course and how long you have studied. Read our [course change page](/study-australia/course-change-in-australia) first.

faqs.q: Can my family come with me?
faqs.a: Only if an exemption applies, and only in the same application. You cannot add them after the student visa is granted. A parent of a student under 18 may still qualify for a guardian visa. See [family on a student visa](/study-australia/student-dependent-visa-500) and the [guardian visa](/study-australia/student-guardian-visa-590).

faqs.q: Do you guarantee a student visa?
faqs.a: No. Only the Department of Home Affairs decides. We tell you honestly how strong your plan looks.

items.x: **Check your timeline.** Count back from your visa end date or your new course start date.
**Log in to your provider's portal.** Submit the CoE request as your provider instructs. Submit once only. Duplicates can slow things down.
**Add supporting documents.** Some changes need evidence, such as a new study plan or medical certificates for compassionate or compelling reasons.
**Update your OSHC.** Extend your Overseas Student Health Cover to cover the new study period.
**Wait for the email.** The CoE is sent to your registered email. Check course, dates and CRICOS code.
**Apply for your visa.** If you need a longer visa, use the new CoE to lodge a Subclass 500 application. See [Student Visa Extension](/study-australia/student-visa-extension).

blocks.x: Your new CoE, OSHC and visa application should all show consistent dates. Mismatches are a common reason for requests for more information. Keep copies of your CoE, OSHC receipt and any supporting documents.
You must lodge your visa application before the course start date on the new CoE.

items.x: Asking for the CoE too close to your visa expiry.
Forgetting to extend OSHC.
Sending several CoE requests.
Moving to a lower-level course without checking whether a new visa is needed.
Leaving a gap between old and new courses.

blocks.x: Check the details, then act on your visa within your timeline. Funds, a Genuine Student statement and health cover will still be needed for a new Subclass 500 application. Check your [funds with the Student Visa Financial Calculator](/study-australia/student-visa-financial-calculator). If you will finish study soon, read about what comes next on [the Study in Australia hub](/study-australia).

faqs.a: Yes, if you are applying for a new Subclass 500 visa for a longer or different course.
